Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images Cop31 Analysis Overseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coal Adam Morton in Nadi, Fiji It isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmine Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Wed 7 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.44 EDT Share There are unlikely to be many bigger moments in Australian community action on the climate crisis this year than a judgment by the high court on Wednesday. In what may prove a historic victory, the court sided with a handful of community members in the Hunter Valley to overturn a state regulator’s approval of a coalmine expansion that allowed it to operate until 2048. This doesn’t happen every day, and the judgment could have ramifications for other coal developments in New South Wales. If comments he made in May are taken at face value, the decision won’t please Anthony Albanese. Speaking on 2HD radio in Newcastle , the prime minister said the renewable transition was needed, but the government supported “existing industries” – that is, coal. He hoped the community group would lose as the Mount Pleasant mine expansion had “been through appropriate approvals”. ‘A real-life moment from The Castle’: the retired Australian couple who took on a coal giant and won Read more Well, not according to the high court. Critics were quick to note the contrast between Albanese’s language opposing legal action to stop a coalmine and the message he delivered over the past three days at a climate conference in Fiji in preparation for the Cop31 summit in Turkey next month. With Pacific island counterparts, the prime minister helped lead a delegation of about 50 dignitaries to the atoll and reef island nation of Tuvalu. Remote and tiny doesn’t do Tuvalu justice. It is described as the least visited country on the planet. Its land totals just 26 sq km, mostly narrow strips less than 2 metres above sea level. And the distance between the ocean and where most of its people live is getting smaller. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The rate of sea level rise around Tuvalu is about twice the global average, according to Nasa researchers. It means the edges of the nation are being eroded. The delegation was given a presentation illustrating the escalating threat of floods and storm surges washing through homes and infrastructure in the years ahead. They also saw an example of what the country is doing to give itself the best chance to survive, visiting a land reclamation project on the main atoll of Funafuti that is mostly funded by the Australian government. Sand and gravel dredged from the lagoon is being used to create more than 20 hectares of new, higher ground. View image in fullscreen Australian PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen, who is the president of the formal negotiations. Photograph: Huang/Menders/Zuma Press Wire Service/Shutterstock It is a project of hope, and a way to buy time. Possibly the most powerful moment on the quick trip came when the delegation was addressed by a 13-year-old, Melelusi Sokotia, who spoke powerfully about how her friends’ aspirations to be “teachers, doctors, builders” was being overridden by the basic question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”. Melelusi made a plea: “Please work together to protect small islands like ours.” Later, back in Fiji, a leaders’ plenary heard from the Nepali foreign affairs minister, Shisir Khanal, who travelled for the pre-Cop meeting while his country staggers under the fallout from devastating flooding in August. It wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiences While the Pacific confronts a crisis of rising tides and more fierce cyclones, Khanal said Nepal was threatened by melting mountain ice bringing havoc from above. He pointed out the two threats were linked. Melting glaciers ultimately add to rising seas. The minister said Nepal and the Pacific had something else in common. Neither contributes much at all to the global emissions causing these catastrophes. “Yet our people pay with their lives and development gains for a crisis they had no hand in creating,” he said. “This is the very definition of climate injustice.” Albanese didn’t ignore this. He took Khanal’s message on enough to repeat part of it – that Nepal faced “extraordinarily traumatic” climate events despite running entirely on hydroelectricity – in a speech before flying out on Wednesday. He described other examples of extreme events becoming less predictable and more intense as “the science told us would occur”. Climate change wasn’t an abstract future challenge, but “a daily reality that communities are dealing with”. “We saw that first-hand yesterday in Tuvalu,” Albanese said. The point of Albanese’s speech was to argue for more international investment in the Pacific Resilience Facility, a fund designed to help people in the region cope and live that has received A$100m in Australian government support. He didn’t mention coal. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion But when held up against his commentary about the high court judgment, it wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiences. Does Albanese disagree with the high court judgment and still support coal expansion, given its contribution to the crisis he has accurately identified? There was no chance to test this on Wednesday. He left pre-Cop without taking questions from journalists. None of this is to dismiss the work being done in Fiji. Despite the focus in Australia on the number of leaders who flew to Nadi and Funafuti for the meeting, there is little sense on the ground of it being the failure some have described. Pre-Cop meetings usually barely make a blip on the public radar. They’re not meant to. They’re a chance for diplomats and bureaucrats to gather before the big end-of-year UN climate summit to lay groundwork and hopefully give it some chance of success. This year is something else entirely. It is being held in the Pacific in an attempt to bring focus to the plight and needs of its peoples. In that, it has had at least some success. Ministers and their representatives from about 50 governments, including India and European nations, attended. So did thousands of diplomats and civil society members. They talked about Pacific needs. Australia faces summer of extreme weather, Anthony Albanese warns at pre-Cop Read more The trip to Tuvalu included only two national leaders from outside the region – but the EU climate commissioner and the heads of the Asian Development Bank, the Green Climate Fund and the UN climate secretariat were on board. They saw and heard things people doing their jobs should see and hear. Pacific national and community leaders are not uniform in their views, but they have largely applauded the focus and Australia’s support. Some are also critical, and cynical, about what they see as Australia’s hypocrisy on fossil fuels. That issue isn’t going away. The ultimate test of this week’s success is whether it helps Cop31 pull off a meaningful agreement on issues to limit climate catastrophe and better direct finance to those that need it to survive, including in the Pacific. To describe that as a challenge in the current geopolitical climate is a spectacular understatement. One upside of this week has been that the two men responsible for trying to pull that off – the president of the formal negotiations, Australia’s Chris Bowen, and the Turkish Cop31 president, Murat Kurum – have had a few days together to build their relationship and consider how they might do that. And they have had a consistent and forceful reminder from those around them of why it matters. Photograph: Mina Kim/Reuters Home Office Surgeon faces deportation as Home Office revokes refugee status for Syrians UK classifies Syria as safe to return to despite UN refugee body’s advice Diane Taylor Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 05.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Syrian plastic surgeon is facing deportation from the UK after the Home Office revoked his refugee status, declaring it is now safe for him and his family to return to their home country. Despite Foreign Office guidance advising against all travel to Syria because of the “volatile” security situation, the government has classified it as a safe place for refugees to return to. Although some European countries are strongly promoting voluntary return to Syria, the Home Office’s decision to actively remove refugee status for Syrians is thought to be the first of its kind in Europe since the fall of the Assad regime. The surgeon, who fled the Assad regime and arrived in the UK in 2016, now lives in London with his wife and six children, three of whom are studying at university. He is understood to be one of the first Syrian refugees in the UK to have his refugee protection cancelled. The move is believed to be the first time the Home Office has cancelled refugee protection for a particular nationality, and thousands of Syrians settled in the UK are likely to be affected. View image in fullscreen People gather in Trafalgar Square in December 2024 after rebels announced that they had ousted Bashar al-Assad in Syria. Photograph: Mina Kim/Reuters “I am so shocked by the Home Office’s decision to withdraw refugee protection,” the surgeon said. “I brought my family to what I considered to be a safe place. We have integrated well but now my refugee status has been cancelled. “I worked as a plastic surgeon in Syria, converted my medical qualifications here so that I am registered with the General Medical Council to work as a doctor here. I am currently working in a GP surgery but am hoping I will be able to continue my practice as a plastic surgeon soon. “I don’t believe Syria will be a safe place for me to return to. I was targeted by certain radical groups in Syria who are still operating there. They are capable of doing many things to me. And I don’t believe that the current Syrian government would be able to protect me from these groups. “I have heard of a few other families who have also had their refugee status taken away from them on the same basis as me – the Home Office says Syria is now a safe country for us to return to. “After I received the letter from the Home Office I delayed telling my family because I wanted to protect them from sadness for a few more days. But now I have given them the news. Like me, they are all in shock and are only just starting to absorb this. My three older children are all studying at university: one is doing neuroscience, another cybersecurity and a third pharmacy. “It’s unsafe for all of us to go back to Syria. By revoking our refugee status the Home Office is depriving us of the right to live our lives.” View image in fullscreen ‘Britain will always provide protection to genuine refugees, and we will never return anyone to danger,’ a Home Office spokesperson said. Photograph: Alex Segre/UCG/Universal Images/Getty Images The Home Office letter states: “Your refugee status has been ceased. Although officials accept that the situation in Syria remains ‘complex’ they consider that changes in Syria are so significant that your fear of persecution and serious harm can no longer be regarded as well founded.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The technical term is “cessation” of refugee status. The UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, in its most recent guidance about the safety of Syria, found that governments should not be returning refugees there. It said: “UNHCR calls on states to refrain from implementing cessation exercises until such time as the situation in Syria has seen significant improvements in overall stability.” Foreign Office guidance states that the security situation in Syria “remains volatile” and adds: “Fighting and violence may occur around the country and is highly unpredictable. This includes artillery and airstrikes.” The guidance also states that there is a humanitarian crisis in Syria including lack of infrastructure, water, sanitation and health services. The family’s solicitor, Manini Menon of Duncan Lewis, said: “It is regrettable that the home secretary has seen fit to target Syrian refugees and their families as part of her pledge to reduce net migration figures. This is a cynical and unprecedented step which will have devastating consequences for a group of people who have rebuilt their lives in the UK with considerable effort, contributing to their communities and putting down roots here. “The evidence in relation to Syria is clear: the circumstances in the country do not allow the home secretary to lawfully conclude that they have stabilised to the extent that refugees can be safely returned there.” The Home Office said: “Britain will always provide protection to genuine refugees, and we will never return anyone to danger. When it is safe for someone to return to their home country, they will be expected to do so. We continue to work closely with governments around the world to develop and maintain returns agreements, including with Syria.” Explore more on these topics Home Office Immigration and asylum Refugees Syria London news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries
